findings.finding: The plan generalises a single icacls reading from 'a Windows runner' to all Windows consumers, and it presumes the key inherits the user profile's ACLs. NTFS ACLs are inherited from the key's actual parent directory. A CI runner's workspace (e.g. a hosted runner's D:\a\ checkout, running as an admin service account) or an explicitly located workspace or server directory outside %USERPROFILE% can inherit very different ACEs from a developer's profile directory. The evidence may therefore not reflect where real consumers' keys live.

findings.finding: Option B ('document that Windows relies on the user profile's default ACLs') assumes the signing key lives where the user profile's default ACLs apply. In the code, the tracker key is `<tracker>/.opcert-key` inside the repository's ticket tracker. The repo can be checked out anywhere, and the key folder's ACL comes from that location, not from the user profile. The plan never checks this location premise.

findings.finding: The 'document the default' option rests on an unchecked claim: that the user profile's default ACLs protect the signing key. The key is written to `<tracker>/.opcert-key`, inside the repository's tracker directory, which can be anywhere (for example C:\src or a shared drive). It is not necessarily under %USERPROFILE%, so profile default ACLs may not apply at all.
scenarios: A repo cloned to C:\work on a multi-user machine: the parent directory grants BUILTIN\Users read by inheritance, so 'profile default ACLs' do not hold.
The Windows runner's checkout sits outside the profile, so the single recorded icacls output does not represent a developer's machine, or the other way round.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a third option to the Approach: rely on and check the ACL that Win32-OpenSSH ssh-keygen applies at creation time. Adopt OpenSSH's Windows private-key rule (owner, SYSTEM, Administrators only; no Users, Authenticated Users or Everyone) as the bar the recorded icacls output is judged against.
evidence: Plan: "Decide whether rebar must restrict the op-cert signing key's access on Windows (an ACL limited to the owner) or document that Windows relies on the user profile's default ACLs."

src/rebar/_opcert_signing.py:103-126: key created via `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N '' -f staging_priv`, then `os.link(staging_priv, key_path)`. A hard link shares the same file, so it keeps the ACL ssh-keygen set.

Retrieved: dev.to 'Using SSH Keys on Windows: Fixing Unprotected Private Key File errors' says that on Windows OpenSSH enforces the check through NTFS ACLs and refuses keys open to Users, Authenticated Users or Everyone, and that only your account plus SYSTEM/Administrators should have access.
Retrieved: Stack Overflow 'Windows CHMOD 600' (5264595) describes the Windows equivalent: turn off inheritance, give the owner full access, remove other entries.
Absence: the plan does not mention OpenSSH's Windows ACL behaviour or give any rule for judging the icacls output.
findings.finding: The plan never considers the established prior art for Windows private-key confidentiality: Win32-OpenSSH's ACL-based equivalent of chmod 600. rebar already relies on it, because the key is created by ssh-keygen and signing goes through ssh-keygen. The plan offers only two options (a rebar-written owner-only ACL, or the user profile's default ACLs). It misses the existing approach: rely on and check the ACL that ssh-keygen applies, and use OpenSSH's acceptable-principal rule as the bar the observed icacls output must meet.
scenarios: The icacls output shows owner, SYSTEM and Administrators only, because ssh-keygen set it. Without a reference rule, the decision-maker may still order a redundant rebar-side ACL implementation.
The icacls output shows inherited Users:(RX). Without OpenSSH's rule as the bar, the reviewer has no stated reason to call this unacceptable.
findings.suggested_fix: In Approach, add: "Option C: rebar already creates the key with Win32-OpenSSH ssh-keygen and publishes it by hard link (same ACL). Record whether ssh-keygen's ACL already meets OpenSSH's own private-key rule (owner + SYSTEM + Administrators, no inherited Users/Authenticated Users/Everyone). If it does, document that and add a Windows check; if it does not, scope an owner-only ACL change." In the AC, state that the icacls output is judged against this rule.
